     To d.ate, the Air Force has undertal:en to investigate and an:llyze .about

     The unexplained reports, hovever, which are in the order of 20 percent of

                         Difficulty in Evaluating ~orts

     The difficulty in disposing of those unexplained roports is based largoly
upon the insufficiency of acc\~ate baSic d.ata such as size, shape, composition
and flight characteristics (speed, acceleration, altitudo, exact maneuver pattern,
etc.) of tho objects.

     Although some instr~ents which are useful 1n obtaining more accurate data
of this type have been available, the reports based on sightinGB with these
instrQ~ents have been very infrequent and comprise an extremely emaIl percentage
of the total. ~breover, o;v"n theecrep:>rts have not included J:luch of the
information required.

     Because of tho inadoquacy of this basic data, the ft~r Forco has in the past
devoted its efforts pr~marily to determining whether these unexplained sightings
indicated the existenco of a menace to the United Ststos. Initially it was
believed that some pattern might evolve froJ:l the study of n large vol\llllo of
reports. To date, no pattern has materialized to reveal anything whatsoever
which can be interpreted as indicative of purpe>se or consistency :>1' which can be
construed as a menace t:> the United States. Nonetheloss, since these unexplained
sightings perSist, the Air Force will continue its investigations, giving the

     It is now fclt, however, thnt reports from poople whose training and
experience in observine aerial objects qualify thom to obtain ess~ntial data
are the only ones likely to produce material suitablo for systematic analysis.
The Air Force is planning to provido additional tools to help these observers
obtain the basic data it needs.

flurries of them in various centuries. The current series of sightings began
generally 1n 1946.
